hints: Recall the side chain R group for each amino acid from the Data Booklet, alanine has $\text{CH}_3$, serine has $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, glycine has $\text{H}$.
Join them in the given order Ala-Ser-Gly with $\text{CO-NH}$ links, keeping a free $\text{NH}_2$ on the left and free $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on the right.
walkthrough:
Picture the three building blocks in order**
Think left to right as N-terminus to C-terminus. Alanine contributes $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO-}$, serine contributes $\text{-NHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO-}$, glycine contributes $\text{-NHCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Glycine is the simplest, its alpha carbon just carries two H atoms.

Link with full peptide bonds**
When $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ condense, water is lost and you get $\text{CO-NH}$. So draw $\text{C=O}$ joined directly to $\text{N-H}$ between residues. Do not abbreviate to CONH, show $\text{CO}$ then $\text{NH}$ explicitly. Keep the terminal $\text{NH}_2$ and terminal $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ untouched.

Final answer: $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO-NHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO-NHCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with both peptide $\text{CO-NH}$ groups shown in full in correct Ala-Ser-Gly sequence.

hints: Add the $M_r$ values of alanine, serine and glycine, then subtract for the two water molecules lost in forming two peptide bonds.
walkthrough:
Account for water loss**
Three free amino acids have $M_r$ values $89 + 105 + 75 = 269$. Forming a tripeptide makes two peptide bonds, so two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules are eliminated.
$$M_r = 89 + 105 + 75 - 2(18) = 233$$

hints: At pH 11 the solution is strongly alkaline, so think which protonated groups $\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ will lose $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Strip the acidic protons**
In neutral solution serine exists largely as the zwitterion $\text{NH}_3^+\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}_2^-$. At pH 11, well above both $pK_a$ values, $\text{OH}^-$ removes the $\text{NH}_3^+$ proton to give neutral $\text{NH}_2$, while the carboxyl stays as $\text{CO}_2^-$. The side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is an alcohol and stays neutral. So you get $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}_2^-$, a singly charged anion.

hints: Start with what must drive ion migration, a voltage source connected to two electrodes.
Decide which electrode is positive by seeing which way the anions moved from the origin.
Recall what the sample is supported on in electrophoresis to keep pH constant.
Match each label F, G, H, I to power supply, anode, cathode and soaked paper or gel.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrical circuit**
F sits in the wires joining the two ends, so it must be the source of potential difference, a DC power supply. It creates a positive end and a negative end.

Assign the electrodes from movement**
All species at pH 11 are anions and they have moved left toward G, so G must attract negative ions. That makes G the positive electrode, the anode. The opposite electrode on the right is the negative electrode, the cathode.

Name the support**
The remaining label for the strip on which the spots sit and the buffer resides is filter paper or gel soaked in buffer solution. The buffer keeps pH at 11 so charge stays constant during migration.

Final answer: F: DC power supply
G: anode or positive electrode
H: filter paper or gel soaked in buffer solution
I: cathode or negative electrode

hints: At pH 11 all amino acids and the peptide carry the same $1-$ charge, so what property other than charge will control distance moved?
Compare the $M_r$ values, glycine is the lightest at $75$ while the tripeptide is the heaviest at $233$.
Link furthest distance from the origin to smallest size and fastest movement, and shortest distance to largest size and slowest movement.
walkthrough:
Fix the charge first**
At pH 11 alanine, serine, glycine and Ala-Ser-Gly are all deprotonated at both the carboxyl and ammonium groups, so each carries a $1-$ charge. That means the electrical pull toward the positive anode is essentially the same for all.

Let size decide the race**
With equal charge, friction with the paper or gel decides. Small ions slip through easily and move fast. Glycine, $M_r = 75$, is the smallest of the four, so it migrates furthest to P. The tripeptide, $M_r = 233$, is much bulkier, experiences most resistance, so it lags behind closest to the origin at S.

Write the identities**
P is therefore glycine anion $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$ and S is the tripeptide anion $[\text{ala-ser-gly}]^-$. Spots Q and R are the intermediate sized alanine and serine.

Final answer: Spot P: glycine, $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$ (or $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$)
Spot S: tripeptide anion, $[\text{ala-ser-gly}]^-$
Glycine is the smallest so travels fastest and furthest toward the anode; tripeptide is the largest so travels slowest and stays closest to the origin.

hints: Breaking peptide amide links back to free amino acids needs heating in aqueous acid or alkali, not just water at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Choose a strong hydrolysis medium**
Peptide $\text{CO-NH}$ bonds are stable amides. Boil or reflux with $6 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HCl}$ to give protonated amino acids, or heat with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ to give carboxylate salts. Either provides $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ plus heat to cleave both peptide bonds.
Final answer: Heat with dilute $\text{HCl}$ ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) under reflux or heat with $\text{NaOH}$($\text{aq}$) ($\text{OH}^-$).

hints: Name the reaction type where water adds across a bond to split a larger molecule into smaller ones.
walkthrough:
Recognise water addition**
Splitting $\text{CO-NH}$ by adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ across each link to regenerate $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ is hydrolysis, the reverse of condensation.
